notes: This source exists for two decisions no other family forces. First, the line carries TWO status codes and TWO body sizes, one per leg, and ECS has one http.response.*; only the value the client actually received is the response. Second, `Duration` is in NANOSECONDS, which is what ECS event.duration wants. Every duration in the training families is in milliseconds or seconds and the correct answer there is to abstain, so a model that has learned to abstain on anything called a duration is wrong here. The inversion is deliberate.

fields.note: `172.18.0.1:47322`. Two values in one string. ECS source.address does not include a port, and the IR has no operation that splits a value, so the two components reach their fields through ClientHost and ClientPort.
Written as a quoted string, not a number. The ECS type is long.
`-` on every line in this capture because no authentication middleware is configured. The placeholder does not change what the field means.
The Host header including the port when the client sent one. Same composite problem as ClientAddr, and RequestHost already carries the domain on its own.
What the CLIENT asked for. Not destination.address: the backend that answers is ServiceAddr, and behind a proxy the two are routinely different names.

`-` whenever the Host header carried no port, which is every line here. url.port would be the field if a value were present, but the client's Host header port is not the port the request was served on.
`HTTP/1.1` on the wire; ECS http.version uses `1.1`. The field is settled, the value convention is not, and normalising it is the parser's job.
A monotonic counter for the Traefik process, not a property of the request. Mapping it to any byte or duration field would be a category error that indexes cleanly.
The backend that actually answered. This is the destination from the proxy's point of view, and it is the field RequestHost is most often confused with.
`app@file`. A Traefik configuration object name, not a network entity.
The backend URL as Traefik configured it, not a URL the client requested. url.original describes what the client asked for.
`app@file`. The name of the Traefik routing rule that matched, qualified by the provider that defined it. rule.name describes a detection or security rule that fired; a routing decision is not one.

The code the BACKEND returned. ECS has one http.response.status_code and it describes the response the client received, which is DownstreamStatus. 0 here whenever Traefik answered without reaching a backend.
The body size the BACKEND returned. The mirror of OriginStatus: ECS has one http.response.body.bytes and it describes what the client received, which is DownstreamContentSize.
Nanoseconds, and a correct unit, but it measures only the backend leg. event.duration is the duration of the event, which is Duration.
Duration minus OriginDuration. A derived figure about the proxy itself.
How many times Traefik retried before an answer was obtained. A property of the proxy's behaviour, not a count of anything in the request or the response.
The code the CLIENT received. This is the response, and it is the one a detection rule filtering on http.response.status_code has to match.
NANOSECONDS, which is exactly what ECS event.duration is. Abstaining here is wrong, and it is the trap this source sets for a model trained on families whose durations are in milliseconds or seconds.
The compression ratio applied to the response, 0 when none was. A ratio, and ECS has no field for one.
`web`. A Traefik listener name. observer.name would describe the appliance rather than one of its listeners, and the log does not name the appliance.
Empty on every access record. ECS `message` is the log message, and an empty string is not one.
